{{For|the astronomer from Geneva|Marcel Golay (astronomer)}}
[[File:Golay Cell Schematic.svg|thumb|alt=Schematic of a Golay cell.|Schematic of a [[Golay cell]]<ref name="Klocke">{{cite journal|last1=Klocke|first1=David|last2=Schmitz|first2=Anke|last3=Soltner|first3=Helmut|last4=Bousack|first4=Herbert|last5=Schmitz|first5=Helmut|title=Infrared receptors in pyrophilous ("fire loving") insects as model for new un-cooled infrared sensors|journal=Beilstein Journal of Nanotechnology|date=30 March 2011|volume=2|pages=186–197|doi=10.3762/bjnano.2.22|pmid=21977430|pmc=3148053}}</ref>]]

'''Marcel Jules Edouard Golay''' ({{IPA|fr|gɔlɛ|lang}}; May 3, 1902 &ndash; April 27, 1989) was a [[Switzerland|Swiss]] [[mathematician]], [[physicist]], and [[information theory|information theorist]], who [[applied mathematics]] to real-world military and industrial problems. He was born in [[Neuchâtel]], [[Switzerland]].<ref name="Massey">{{cite journal|last1=Massey|first1=James L.|title=MARCEL J.E. GOLAY (1902-1989) obituary|journal=IEEE Information Society Newsletter|date=1990|volume=June|url=http://www.astrohandbook.com/Obit_by_Massey.pdf|access-date=2016-03-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181215223129/http://www.astrohandbook.com/Obit_by_Massey.pdf|archive-date=2018-12-15|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Career==
Golay studied [[electrical engineering]] at the Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule ([[ETH Zurich|Swiss Federal Institute of Technology]]) in [[Zürich]].  He joined [[Bell laboratories]] in [[New York City]] in 1924, spending four years there. He received a Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1931.<ref name="CHFPapers">{{cite web|title=Finding Aid to Marcel J. E. Golay, 1931-2002 (bulk 1946-1989)|url=http://othmerlib.sciencehistory.org/record=b1071980~S6|website=[[Science History Institute]] |quote="Click on 'Golay Box List' to go to full list."|publisher=Science History Institute}}</ref>

Golay then joined the [[US Army Signal Corps]], eventually rising to the post of Chief Scientist. He was based mostly in [[Fort Monmouth]], [[New Jersey]]. He developed an IR "radar" based on its [[Golay Detector]], the SCR-268T specifically designed to the detection of vessels (S/S Normandie was detected at its inaugural crossing). The SCR-268 (using Barkausen vacuum tubes) and the SCR-268T were to work together. However the 268T, only used in the Pacific theater was abandoned before the end of the war.<ref name="CHFPapers"/>

Between 1955 and 1963, Golay was a consultant for Philco Corporation of Philadelphia, PA, and the Perkin-Elmer Corporation of Norwalk, Connecticut. In 1963, Golay joined the [[Perkin-Elmer]] company full-time as senior research scientist.<ref name="CHFPapers"/> Golay worked on many problems, including [[gas chromatography]] and [[optical spectroscopy]]. It was during this period when he patented an Analysis of Images, for two-dimensional parallel data processing, and worked to develop the idea, called Golay Logic for Optical Pattern Recognition along with Kendall Preston, Philip Norgren, David Dacava and [[Joseph Carvalko, Jr.]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://patft.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO2&Sect2=HITOFF&u=%2Fnetahtml%2FPTO%2Fsearch-adv.htm&r=1&p=1&f=G&l=50&d=PTXT&S1=4,060,713.PN.&OS=PN/4,060,713&RS=PN/4,060,713 |title=Patent Database Search Results: PN/4,060,713 in US Patent Collection| website=patft.uspto.gov}}</ref> He remained with Perkin-Elmer for the rest of his life.

==Achievements==
*Discoverer of the famous [[Binary Golay code|binary]] and [[Ternary Golay code|ternary]] Golay codes, which are perfect [[Error correction codes|error-correcting codes]] that generalize the [[Hamming code]]. They were used in the [[Binary Golay code#NASA deep space missions|Voyager]] probes, and led to advances in the theory of [[finite groups]].
*Co-author with [[Abraham Savitzky]] of the [[Savitzky–Golay filter]]. 
*Inventor of the [[Golay cell]], a type of [[infrared]] detector.
*He introduced [[complementary sequences]]. Those are pairs of [[binary sequence]]s whose autocorrelation functions add up to zero for all non-zero time shifts. Today they are used in various WiFi and 3G standards.
*He introduced the theory of dispersion in open tubular columns (capillary columns) and demonstrated their efficacy at the Second International Symposium on Gas Chromatography at Amsterdam in 1958.<ref name="Vapor">{{cite journal|last1=Golay|first1=M. J. E.|title=Vapor Phase Chromatography and Telegrapher's Equation|journal=Anal. Chem.|date=1957|volume=29|issue=6|pages=928–932|doi=10.1021/ac60126a019}}</ref>
